I’ll compare NetHack’s strongest design ideas against JSHack’s current architecture and content surfaces, then separate “worth bringing over,” “better modernized,” and “probably leave behind.” I’m going to use the repo’s provenance-aware exploration guidance and inspect the current game structure before making recommendations.

The repo already has several NetHack-adjacent seeds—pets, corpses, altars/deities, traps, shops, engraving, polymorph, genocide, and hidden-ish interactions—so the useful question is less “what classic feature is missing?” and more “which NetHack systems could deepen JSHack’s existing loops without turning it into a compatibility project.” I’m checking NetHack’s canonical feature set now, including the parts that create its famous emergent stories.

content.text:
NetHack is worth mining for design ideas, but not copying whole. Its best legacy is the way a small set of rules produces memorable, player-authored stories.

JSHack already has surprisingly much of the foundation:

- Pets with guarding, aggression, threat redirection, taming, fetching, and corpse consequences.
- Deities, prayer, altars, offerings, wrath, miracles, and patron shifts.
- Shops with debt, ownership, enforcement, perception, and witness-based escape.
- Traps, engraving, corpses, corpse-derived abilities, polymorph, genocide, identification, hunger, and procedural dungeon branches.

That means the best additions are “system multipliers,” not isolated NetHack features.

## Highest-value ideas to bring over

### 1. Conducts, achievements, and end-of-run history

This is probably the best low-cost/high-impact addition.

NetHack tracks unusual constraints such as pacifist, atheist, illiterate, vegetarian, wishless, weaponless, and no-polymorph runs. It also records milestones like entering shops, temples, mines, Sokoban, defeating major bosses, acquiring artifacts, and reaching the endgame. The official guide explicitly treats these as persistent bragging rights and challenge structures. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

For JSHack, this could become:

- “Never killed a humanoid”
- “Never used a shrine”
- “No consumable healing”
- “Never left the overworld”
- “Only one companion”
- “No identified items”
- “No direct damage spells”
- “Never entered a shop”
- “Pacifist until betrayed”
- “Completed a dungeon without resting”

This gives players reasons to experiment with the systems already present. It also creates a natural end-of-run summary without requiring a rigid achievement tree.

Recommendation: build a generic event-backed conduct ledger before adding more content.

### 2. Distinctive artifacts with verbs, not just better stats

NetHack artifacts are memorable because they change how you play: special resistances, alignment interactions, transformations, teleportation, life-saving, monster hatred, and invokable powers. The quest artifacts are especially strong because they are tied to role identity and optional dungeon branches. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

JSHack should add a small number of authored artifacts with:

- A strong identity and backstory.
- A unique passive.
- An explicit `invoke` or alternate-use action.
- A cost, danger, alignment consequence, or social consequence.
- A reason to carry it even when another item has higher raw stats.

Examples:

- A sword that grows stronger when fighting creatures that have harmed your pet.
- A lantern that reveals secret doors but attracts enemies while lit.
- A shrine relic that lets you change patron deity once, permanently angering the old one.
- A ring that grants polymorph control but slowly makes the wearer less stable.
- A staff that can teleport you to a known landmark, but ages or damages the dungeon.

Recommendation: 8–12 excellent artifacts, not 100 generic uniques.

### 3. Optional branches with their own rules

NetHack’s branches matter because they are not merely different art sets. Sokoban changes movement rules and tracks violations; Mines’ End and other branches offer unique exploration incentives. The guidebook specifically treats Sokoban’s rules and prize as a separate challenge. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

JSHack already has the dungeon/template machinery to support this. The next step would be branches where the environment changes the rules:

- A boulder-and-pressure-plate puzzle branch.
- A flooded branch where sound, electricity, and movement behave differently.
- A shrine branch where combat affects deity alignment.
- A “living dungeon” branch that remembers theft, fire, and destroyed rooms.
- A branch where monsters are mostly peaceful until the player violates local customs.

Each should have:

1. One memorable rule.
2. One unique reward.
3. One optional risk.
4. A way to understand the rule through play.

Recommendation: one polished “Sokoban successor” branch before adding many more dungeon floors.

### 4. Deeper pet ecology

NetHack pets are not just friendly combat summons. Their hunger, loyalty, trap avoidance, fetching, equipment use, growth, abuse, death, and revival create stories. The pet system even makes companions respond differently to cursed items, dangerous enemies, traps, and food. [NetHack Pet reference](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/Pet)

JSHack already has the right architecture and some of the right behavior. Good next additions would be:

- Pet hunger and preferred foods.
- Pet trust/tameness as a gradual value rather than a binary state.
- Pet fear and retreat thresholds.
- Pets refusing dangerous targets based on passive attacks.
- Pets recognizing and avoiding known traps.
- A whistle/bell/leash-style control item.
- Pet death and revival with changed loyalty.
- Smart pets using a small set of appropriate items.

The key is not adding pet micromanagement. The goal is for the player to think, “I lost because I brought my wolf into the wrong room,” or “my cat saved the run by refusing to attack that creature.”

### 5. Identification as a central knowledge game

NetHack’s unidentified objects are powerful because identification is not just an inventory UI feature. It creates uncertainty, experimentation, risk, and player knowledge. The official guide emphasizes that item identity is learned through use and observation. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/download/5.0.0/nethack-500-Guidebook.pdf)

JSHack already has an identification system, so the successor version could deepen it with:

- Partial identification: “this potion is probably restorative.”
- Reliable visual, smell, or behavior clues.
- Item histories: “this wand killed a goblin,” “this ring caused polymorph.”
- Identification through NPCs, shops, deities, and experimentation.
- Cursed-item suspicion based on behavior rather than immediate disclosure.
- Run knowledge versus character knowledge, if desired.

Recommendation: make discovery feel like a playable investigation, while keeping the UI readable and fair.

## Ideas to borrow carefully

### Wishes

Wishes are powerful because they let players solve a specific missing problem, but in NetHack they can also become an optimization checklist for an “ascension kit.” The wish system is one of the game’s recognized challenge axes. [NetHack wish/conduct references](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/What_to_wish_for)

For JSHack, I would avoid literal unlimited item wishes. Better variants:

- A deity grants one “boon request” with ambiguous wording.
- A djinn offers three imperfect choices.
- A relic lets you name a category, not an exact item.
- A wish always creates a debt, curse, enemy, or future obligation.
- Wishes can request an escape, knowledge, companion, or transformation—not just equipment.

### Bones files and dead-player ghosts

NetHack’s dead adventurer remnants are cool, but they create persistence and fairness questions. A lighter JSHack version could preserve only a “death echo”:

- A named ghost or hostile remnant appears in a future run.
- It uses a small sample of the dead character’s equipment.
- It leaves behind a clue, curse, or one item.
- It is deterministic from the run seed.

This fits JSHack’s tombstone/death infrastructure better than importing full persistent level files.

### Genocide

JSHack already has genocide-like machinery. It is a good example of a feature that should remain rare and consequential, not become routine monster filtering. Its best use is as a desperate strategic choice with ecological consequences: remove one threat, but alter loot, food, quests, or deity reactions.

## What I would not bring over directly

- NetHack’s extreme exception density and opaque rules.
- Literal hunger micromanagement for the player.
- Huge role-specific artifact catalogs.
- Mandatory spoiler knowledge.
- Permanent run deaths caused by obscure item interactions with no warning.
- A giant ASCII-command vocabulary.
- Branches that exist only to add more floors and monsters.
- “Everything can interact with everything” without a readable feedback layer.

The successor should preserve NetHack’s emergent depth while making the causal chain visible enough that players can learn through play.

## My suggested successor direction

The strongest identity for JSHack would be:

> A readable, visual NetHack successor where the world remembers what you do, companions have real agency, religions react to your behavior, and optional challenges become part of your run history.

The first three systems I would prioritize are:

1. A conduct/achievement ledger.
2. A small artifact-and-invocation framework.
3. One deeply authored optional branch with a unique rule and reward.

Those would amplify the existing pets, deities, shops, corpses, identification, and dungeon systems rather than competing with them.
you read nothing about jshack

Fair criticism. I looked at the repo, but I gave you a generic NetHack design essay instead of demonstrating that I understood JSHack’s actual shape. I’m going to correct that by grounding the comparison in the current player loop, world structure, content catalog, and existing systems—then I’ll tell you which NetHack ideas are actually missing or redundant.

You’re right. I read the repo, but my answer didn’t reflect it. I treated JSHack like a generic roguelike and recommended features it already has.

The actual JSHack shape is much more specific:

- It is a mobile-first, touch-driven game, not an ASCII-command adaptation.
- It has a persistent-feeling overworld village with shops, townfolk roles, farming, seasons, weather, economy chains, reputation, and faction trouble.
- It already has 9 classes, 58 monsters, 338 catalog items, 64 spells, 34 affixes, 69 effects, pets, deities, hunger, encumbrance, crafting, fishing, cooking, traps, polymorph, genocide, corpses, engraving, shop law, quests, and multi-floor biome dungeons.
- Its central design promise is “readable chaos”: systems should surprise the player, but remain learnable.
- Its strongest existing pattern is that new behavior falls out of shared systems: perception, threat, reputation, deity mood, item procs, corpses, weather, water, fire, and town simulation.

So yes: pets, altars, shops, corpses, polymorph, traps, identification, and deity reactions were bad recommendations as “missing features.” They are already core JSHack material.

The genuinely interesting NetHack ideas for JSHack are narrower:

1. Conducts should become a first-class layer over existing events.

JSHack already has the ingredients for a much richer run identity: deity actions, theft, pet treatment, corpse eating, spell use, faction offenses, crafting, quest choices, and town consequences. NetHack’s conduct system tracks things like pacifism, atheism, illiteracy, and wishlessness as alternate ways to play, not just achievements. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

For JSHack, this could produce run identities such as:

- never harmed a townsperson
- never abandoned a pet
- never used a shrine
- never ate a corpse
- never used direct-damage magic
- never entered a shop
- never slept in a bed
- never descended below a certain dungeon depth
- completed a quest while aligned with a hostile faction

That would reinforce existing systems rather than add a parallel progression track.

2. Artifacts should be cross-system objects.

JSHack has a huge item catalog and affix system, but I did not find a clearly central artifact/invocation layer comparable to NetHack’s role artifacts and unique item verbs.

The right JSHack artifact would not merely be “a stronger sword.” It would connect systems:

- a weapon that gains power from defending pets
- a relic that changes how a deity judges offerings
- a lantern that reveals hidden terrain but increases monster attention
- a tool that can alter weather or water at a cost
- an item that can rescue you from a dungeon but permanently damages town reputation

NetHack’s strongest artifacts modify the player’s available decisions, which is more relevant to JSHack than copying its item names or stat bonuses. [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

3. Dungeon branches should change rules, not just scenery.

JSHack already has an overworld return, multi-floor dungeons, biome slices, underworld templates, stairs, traps, boulders, and authored quest destinations. A NetHack-style branch would be valuable only if it introduces a local law:

- a branch where sound attracts creatures through walls
- a flooded branch where electricity and movement behave differently
- a shrine branch where killing changes the level’s deity alignment
- a boulder/puzzle branch where pets and monsters affect the puzzle
- a branch where every stolen object creates a persistent local response

Sokoban is useful as a model because it has its own movement rules and a distinct reward, not because JSHack needs “a puzzle level.” [NetHack Guidebook](https://www.nethack.org/v500/Guidebook.html)

4. Pet ecology is the most promising existing JSHack system to deepen.

JSHack already has pet behavior, guarding, aggro protection, taming, fetching, pet commands, pet corpses, and deity consequences around pets. NetHack’s pets become stories because they have hunger, loyalty, trap preferences, fear, item behavior, growth, abuse, and imperfect judgment. [NetHack Pet reference](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/Pet)

The next useful additions would be:

- trust/tameness as a gradual relationship
- food preferences and hunger
- fear and retreat behavior
- refusal to attack obviously dangerous targets
- known-trap avoidance
- whistles, leashes, or treats as control tools
- revival with altered loyalty

That is much more “JSHack” than importing another class or another dungeon monster.

5. Wishes should probably become deity bargains.

JSHack already has deities, patron shifts, prayer, wrath, offerings, miracles, and challenge behavior. NetHack wishes are powerful, but they can collapse into an equipment-optimization checklist. [NetHack wish reference](https://nethackwiki.com/wiki/What_to_wish_for)

A JSHack version should be:

- ask a deity for help
- choose between several imperfect interpretations
- incur a debt, vow, curse, reputation cost, or future obligation
- possibly ask for knowledge, escape, a companion, or a world change—not only an item

That would fit the current deity architecture much better than a generic djinn/wish system.

6. Death echoes are a better fit than full NetHack bones files.

JSHack already has tombstones, death effects, post-mortem behavior, save/load infrastructure, and deterministic seeds. A lightweight “dead adventurer echo” could leave behind:

- a named hostile remnant
- one remembered item
- a curse or clue
- a local change in the dungeon

That would give runs a relationship with prior failures without requiring persistent level-file machinery.

The corrected conclusion is:

JSHack should not become “NetHack with graphics.” It is already evolving into a reactive overworld-and-dungeon simulation. The NetHack successor opportunity is to add:

- conduct-driven run identity,
- cross-system artifacts,
- rule-changing dungeon branches,
- deeper companion ecology,
- and deity-mediated bargains.

Those are the parts that would amplify JSHack’s existing gravity.
propose one change please

Add a “Run Vows” system inspired by NetHack conducts.

At character creation, the player may optionally choose one vow:

- never kill a humanoid
- never use direct-damage spells
- never abandon a pet
- never pray
- never steal
- never eat corpses

The rules layer records vow-breaking events, and the run summary reports whether each vow survived. Completing a vow grants a small thematic reward—reputation, deity favor, a title, or a unique end-of-run score multiplier.

Why this one: JSHack already emits and tracks nearly everything needed—kills, spells, pets, shops, prayer, corpses, quests, factions—so it would turn existing systems into alternate playstyles with relatively little new machinery. It also fits JSHack’s “readable chaos” better than copying NetHack’s opaque item interactions.

content.text:
Agreed. I removed character-creation vows.

Now the game passively tracks the run and derives end-screen honors:

- Pacifist
- Spellless
- Prayerless
- Honest hands
- Corpse-pure

The death screen currently looks structurally like this:

```text
              ☠️

          Mara Has Perished

Class: Mireborn
Slain by: the drowned archivist
Depth reached: 7
Score: 1840
Gold: 142g
Turns survived: 1260 (2 days)
Spells learned: 9
Weapon: Ashen Hook
Devoted to: The River Below
Status: wet, bleeding

Run Chronicle
Honors: Prayerless · Honest hands · Corpse-pure
Kills: 18
Spells cast: 9
Prayers: 0
Shop escapes: 0
Pets lost: 0
Pet corpses desecrated: 0

Seed: 0xC0FFEE | v0.9.1400

Global Highscores
...

Share details
[x] Honors          [x] Traits
[x] Weapon          [x] Deity
[x] Spells          [x] Status effects
[x] Run chronicle

☠️ Share Your Death
🔒 Copy Score Proof
⚔ New Game
```

The share checkboxes dynamically regenerate the X post. For example, with only honors and the chronicle selected:

```text
☠️ Mara the Mireborn died by the drowned archivist on depth 7
1840 pts | 142 gold | 1260 turns
Honors: Prayerless, Honest hands, Corpse-pure
18 kills | 0 prayers | 0 pets lost

#JSHack
```

There is currently one combined death/share screen rather than a separate `shareDeath` modal. I attempted to capture a browser screenshot, but the available headless Firefox crashed while loading the preview, so I’m showing the actual rendered layout as a wireframe here.

The passive chronicle implementation is in [runHonors.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/data/runHonors.js), [runChronicleSystem.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/runChronicleSystem.js), and [overlayUtils.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/display/ui/overlayUtils.js). Focused tests pass: 6/6.
